headline: High-risk shared-workflow pair: Langflow’s unsandboxed server-side execution and broad egress create dangerous default paths for leakage, conflict, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no direct I/O surfaces and no network egress, so it cannot itself ingest B’s outputs by default. B can read/write files and chain agents in flows, and its server-side graph can treat file content as flow input. The pair therefore has a plausible shared-workspace bridge, but the exact bridge is not documented here, so uncertainty is escalated to medium.
conditions: IF both agents are connected through a shared filesystem or uploaded-file handoff, A’s content can be interpreted as instructions by B.
IF B ingests A-generated text without provenance checks, prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Disable shared folders between the two agents.
Route A outputs through a plain-text sanitizer before B reads them.
Require provenance labels on all files passed into B.
Use separate workspaces per flow run.
requires-engineering: add content-type and trust-boundary checks in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no egress, which limits direct leakage from A. B touches flow inputs and intermediate outputs, reads the filesystem, and has broad network egress to model providers and arbitrary HTTP services. If A and B share files or a workspace, B can exfiltrate whatever A writes. The shared-workspace pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF A writes sensitive content into a directory B can read, B can transmit it to external services.
IF both agents are run under the same workspace or account, leakage risk increases materially.
mitigations: Separate storage locations for each agent.
Restrict B’s outbound destinations to an allowlist.
Turn off file uploads in B for sensitive runs.
Rotate any credentials stored in B after shared runs.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on the workspace.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A is an open-source agent hub with MCP/agent tooling, while B can execute shell commands, install packages, write the filesystem, and spawn subprocesses. B also uses server-side shared state across instances. If both operate on the same directory or repo, concurrent writes and environment changes can collide and corrupt state. Because B’s defaults are powerful and the shared target is plausible, high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or repository, file clobbering can occur.
IF B installs packages or mutates the runtime while A assumes a stable environment, runs can diverge or fail.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Freeze dependencies before running B.
Disable concurrent runs against the same repo.
Use file locks around shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B is a graph-based orchestrator that can chain multiple agents and wire tools into flow nodes, so it may treat upstream outputs as authoritative unless explicitly checked. A is an agent hub/RAG-style source that can emit generated content for downstream use. That creates a default pathway where A’s output becomes B’s input and then drives further actions, making cascading mistakes likely and potentially irreversible.
conditions: IF B routes A-generated text into downstream tools without validation, errors can propagate.
IF B’s flow includes action-taking nodes, a mistaken A output can trigger external side effects.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before action nodes.
Require schema validation on A outputs.
Mark A outputs as untrusted in B.
Disable auto-execution for flows that consume A.
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agent nodes.

E_compliance.rationale: A is open-source and does not show touched regulated data classes, while B stores per-flow credentials and processes flow inputs/intermediate outputs. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance concern is visible: B’s handling of secrets and flow data may exceed A’s minimal footprint. The other agent is cited because the pairwise workflow determines where data lands.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through B’s flows, retention and logging controls must match that data class.
IF A is used as a source for secrets or personal data, B’s storage policy becomes relevant.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data into B.
Review B retention settings before each run.
Store secrets outside flow state where possible.
Purge flow histories after testing.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls for the deployment.
